archives.title: M-Pesa Launch
archives.body:
In March 2007, Safaricom launched M-Pesa — a mobile money transfer service that would change Kenya forever. The idea was simple: send money using your phone, no bank account needed.

At first, people were sceptical. Cash was king. Banks were for the rich. But M-Pesa solved a real problem: millions of Kenyans in cities needed to send money home to family in rural areas. Before M-Pesa, you'd hand cash to a bus driver heading upcountry and pray it arrived.

Within a year, M-Pesa had over a million users. Within a decade, it processed more transactions than Western Union did globally. It turned kiosk owners into bankers and phones into wallets.

Kenya didn't just adopt mobile money — it invented the model the world would copy.
sources: The Economist, 'Why does Kenya lead the world in mobile money?' (2015)

archives.title: Matatu Culture
archives.body:
Matatus are more than transport — they're Nairobi's heartbeat. These privately owned minibuses are cultural statements on wheels: hand-painted murals of musicians, footballers, and movie stars; booming sound systems; LED lighting rigs that would shame a nightclub.

The word 'matatu' likely comes from 'mang'otore matatu' — the original three-cent fare. Each matatu has a driver and a conductor (makanga) who collects fares, calls out stops, and performs feats of acrobatics hanging from the doorframe.

Matatus have their own names, their own followings, their own rivalries. The Nairobi routes are legendary — and so is the driving. The government has tried to regulate them for decades, with mixed results. Love them or fear them, matatus ARE Nairobi.

The matatu industry is one of Kenya's largest informal employers, supporting hundreds of thousands of families.
sources: Mutongi, K. 'Matatu: A History of Popular Transportation in Nairobi' (2017)
